questions.q: What is decomposition?
questions.explain: Nobody can write "a banking app" in one go. Decomposition splits it into users, accounts, transfers and so on, then splits each of those, until every piece is one clear step.
options: Deleting the parts of a program you no longer need
Breaking a big problem into smaller problems, and those into smaller ones, until each piece is clear enough to solve
Translating source code into machine code
Running a program many times with different inputs

questions.q: When is a piece small enough to stop splitting?
questions.explain: Those three questions tell you the piece is one job, well defined, and checkable. "Is the amount more than 0?" passes all three. "Check the request" does not: it checks the owner and the amount and the balance.
options: When it fits on one screen
When it has exactly three sub-pieces
When it can be said in one sentence without "and", has a known input and output, and can be tested on its own
When a senior programmer approves it

questions.q: Which of these pieces most clearly needs to be split further?
questions.explain: Its description needs two "and"s: it is three jobs. Each of the others is a single step with a clear input and output.
options: Is the cart empty?
Add the delivery fee to the price
Check the order and take the payment and tell the kitchen
Save the order with status "received"

questions.q: Which of these is a good leaf of the "Check the request" part of a transfer?
questions.explain: A leaf is one clear step: here, a single comparison with a yes or no answer. "Make it secure" and "Handle the money" are goals, not steps; each still needs splitting.
options: Handle the money
Is A's balance at least the amount?
Make the transfer secure
Transfers

questions.q: What is top-down design?
questions.explain: Top-down starts at the top of the tree ("banking application") and works down to the leaves. It is the best way to understand a problem and make sure nothing is forgotten.
options: Starting from the whole problem and splitting it level by level until you reach steps you can write
Writing the first line of the program first and the last line last
Building small pieces first and combining them later
Testing the biggest feature before the smallest

questions.q: Which of these is an example of working bottom-up?
questions.explain: Bottom-up starts from small pieces you know you need, makes them work, and combines them into bigger features. The fee piece was tested at its boundaries first, then used by the transfer check.
options: Drawing the whole decomposition tree before writing anything
Building and testing the transfer-fee piece before any transfer code exists, then plugging it in
Asking the chairman what the app must do
Splitting "Transfers" into four parts

questions.q: What does "design top-down, build bottom-up" mean in practice?
questions.explain: Top-down finds all the pieces and how they connect. Bottom-up building means every piece you combine already works. Real teams use both.
options: Only senior programmers design; only juniors build
Draw the tree from the top so every piece is known, then build and test the leaves first and combine them upwards
Design and build the top level first, and never build the leaves
Build everything, then draw a tree of what you built

questions.q: What is the main risk of working only top-down?
questions.explain: Top-down is good at not forgetting pieces, but if you only ever plan, nothing runs until the very end, and problems in the plan show up late. Building leaves early catches them sooner.
options: Pieces that nobody needed
A detailed plan, but nothing working and tested for a long time
Forgetting important pieces
Too many tests

questions.q: What is the main risk of working only bottom-up?
questions.explain: Without a top-down picture, you can build a beautiful fee calculator in the wrong currency, or a notifications piece that expects data no other piece provides.
options: Well-made pieces that do not fit together, or that the problem never needed
Nothing ever gets tested
The pieces are always too big
You cannot write any code until the plan is finished

questions.q: What does "Transfers depends on Accounts" mean?
questions.explain: A transfer moves money between accounts. Without the Accounts piece there is nothing to move money between, so Accounts is built first.
options: Transfers must be built before Accounts
Transfers cannot work without Accounts, so Accounts must exist first
Accounts and Transfers are the same piece
Accounts calls Transfers every time a balance changes

questions.q: A shop system has: Products (needs nothing), Customers (needs nothing), Cart (needs Products, Customers), Orders (needs Cart), Receipts (needs Orders). Which build order works?
questions.explain: Each piece must come after everything it needs. Cart needs both Products and Customers, so both must come before it. The last option builds Cart before Customers.
options: Cart, Products, Customers, Orders, Receipts
Receipts, Orders, Cart, Customers, Products
Customers, Products, Cart, Orders, Receipts
Products, Cart, Customers, Orders, Receipts

questions.q: In the bank, Authentication needs only Users, and Accounts needs only Users. Once Users is built, what does that tell you?
questions.explain: Neither needs the other, only Users. So once Users exists, they can be built in parallel, by different people, in either order.
options: Authentication must be built before Accounts
Accounts must be built before Authentication
Two people can build Authentication and Accounts at the same time
The two pieces should be merged

questions.q: Your plan says piece A needs piece B, and piece B needs piece A. What does that usually mean?
questions.explain: With a circle, neither piece can be built or tested first. Moving the shared part into its own piece, which both can use, removes the circle.
options: The plan is perfect: the pieces work closely together
Build A first, B second
The split is in the wrong place: part of A and part of B probably belong together in a piece of their own
Nothing: circles are normal in every design

questions.q: The notifications piece only needs a phone number and a message; it knows nothing about transfers. Why is that good?
questions.explain: The fewer things a piece needs from others, the safer it is to change. A piece with small, clear needs can be replaced without anything else noticing.
options: It makes SMS messages shorter
When the SMS company changes, only the notifications piece changes; no transfer code is touched
It means notifications never fail
It lets notifications move money

questions.q: A transfer subtracts ₦15,000 from account A, then the server crashes before adding it to account B. What is the problem, and what does the plan need?
questions.explain: "Move the money" is two leaves that are not independent. The plan must say they succeed or fail together. Databases provide this with a transaction, which you will use later.
options: No problem: B will get the money when the server restarts
The fee was wrong, so the plan needs a new fee piece
The money has vanished; the two steps must happen together or not at all
A's owner must be logged out

questions.q: A slow network makes a member tap "Send ₦15,000" twice, and both requests arrive. Which missing leaf would stop ₦30,000 from moving?
questions.explain: Both requests pass every normal check. Giving each transfer request a unique reference, and refusing a second request with the same reference, is the leaf the first tree forgot.
options: Is the amount more than 0?
Send an SMS to both people
Have we already done a request with this reference number?
Is the person logged in?

questions.q: The money moved correctly, but the SMS company is down. What should happen to the transfer?
questions.explain: Moving the money is essential; the SMS is "best effort". Notifications are a separate piece so that their failure does not undo a correct transfer and can be retried.
options: Undo the transfer, because the member was not told
Keep the transfer; send the SMS later, when the SMS company is back
Send the money a second time
Stop the whole bank until SMS works again

questions.q: Why does the transfer check "does this person own account A?" before "is A's balance big enough?"
questions.explain: With else if, only the first failed check is reported. If the balance came first, a stranger trying to send from Ada's account would get "not enough money" or not, which leaks information about her balance.
options: Because it is shorter to write
Otherwise someone else could learn whether A has enough money from the refusal message
Because JavaScript checks conditions from bottom to top
The order of checks never matters

questions.q: The withdrawal piece checks amount <= balance. The transfer piece has its own copy that checks amount < balance. What is the best fix?
questions.explain: The bug exists because the same rule lives in two places and the copies drifted apart. One shared piece means one rule, fixed and tested once.
options: Delete the withdrawal check
Add a comment saying the two are different
Make "has enough money" one piece, in one place, and have both withdrawals and transfers use it
Change both to amount === balance

questions.q: Why is it better to split an app by job (check, move, record, tell) than by screen (home page, send money page)?
questions.explain: "You can only send from your own account" is a rule of the job, not of one page. Split by job, and every screen becomes a thin layer on top of the same, tested pieces.
options: Screens are harder to draw
The rules must hold however the request arrives: phone app, website or a bank officer's computer all use the same pieces
Users never see screens
Splitting by job makes the app load faster

questions.q: Which of these is an integration test rather than a unit test?
questions.explain: A unit test checks one piece alone. "A refused transfer leaves both balances unchanged" checks that the check piece and the move piece work correctly together: that is a test of the join.
options: The fee piece gives ₦10 for ₦5,000
The amount check refuses 0
A refused transfer leaves both balances unchanged
The daily limit piece allows exactly ₦100,000

questions.q: In large systems, where do most serious failures happen?
questions.explain: Small pieces are easy to test completely. The trouble comes where pieces meet: one succeeds and the next fails, or one sends data the other does not expect. Plan the arrows as carefully as the boxes.
options: Inside the smallest leaves
At the joins between pieces, such as a payment that succeeds while saving the record fails
In the comments
In the first line of each file

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Ada owns the account and the amount is positive, so the first two checks pass. ₦10,000 is more than ₦8,000, so the third sets the problem. The move never runs.
options: Sent. Balance: ₦-2000
Refused: not enough money
Refused: you do not own this account
Refused: none

questions.q: Two checks fail here. What does it print?
questions.explain: With else if, once one condition is true, the rest are skipped. The ownership check is first and fails, so only its message is set.
options: you do not own this account
the amount must be more than 0

you do not own this account
the amount must be more than 0
none

questions.q: Fees: ₦10 up to ₦5,000, ₦25 up to ₦50,000, ₦50 above. What does this print?
questions.explain: 5,000 is "up to 5,000", so ₦10. 50,000 fails the first test but passes <= 50000, so ₦25. 60,000 fails both and keeps the starting value, ₦50.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The fee for ₦9,990 is ₦25, so the transfer needs ₦10,015, more than the ₦10,000 balance. Without the fee piece the check would have passed. Adding one piece changed what another piece must check.
options: Sent. Balance: ₦10
Refused: need ₦10015
Sent. Balance: ₦-15
Refused: need ₦10000

questions.explain: 20000 <= 20000 is true, but 20000 < 20000 is false. The same rule, written twice, gives two answers. That is why a rule should live in one piece.

Withdrawal: allowed
Transfer: refused

questions.explain: 95,000 + 5,000 is exactly 100,000, which is not more than 100,000, so it is allowed. Only 6,000 takes the total over. The test list sits exactly around the boundary.
options:
4000 allowed
5000 over the limit
6000 over the limit

questions.explain: The check fails, so problem is not "none" and the move piece is skipped entirely. A refused transfer leaves both balances as they were.

questions.explain: amount <= 0 is true for -100 and for 0, so both are refused. problem is reset to "none" at the start of each round, so 100 is not affected by the earlier ones.
options:
-100 -> must be more than 0
0 -> must be more than 0

questions.q: This simulates a crash between the two steps of a transfer. What does it print?
questions.explain: The subtraction ran, the addition did not. The total money in the bank dropped by ₦15,000: it vanished. That is why the two steps must happen together or not at all.
options:
Money before: 62000
Money after: 62000

Money before: 62000
Money after: 47000

Money before: 62000
Money after: 77000

Money before: 62000
Money after: 35000

questions.q: The same request arrives twice. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first time, lastReference is empty, so the money moves and the reference is remembered. The second request has the same reference, so it is refused. ₦15,000 moves once, as the member intended.
options:
Sent. Balance: 35000
Sent. Balance: 20000

Sent. Balance: 35000
Already done: TX-7

Already done: TX-7
Already done: TX-7
Sent. Balance: 35000

questions.q: The check piece is missing its first leaf. Add a check, before the balance check, that sets problem to "you do not own this account" when loggedInUser is not fromOwner. With the inputs given, it must print Refused: you do not own this account.
questions.explain: !== means "is not equal to". Putting the ownership check first, with the balance check as else if, means a stranger never learns anything about the balance.
questions.expected: Refused: you do not own this account

questions.q: A member can "send" ₦0, or even a negative amount, which would add money to their own account. Add a leaf that sets problem to "the amount must be more than 0" when the amount is 0 or less. With the inputs given, it must print Refused: the amount must be more than 0.
questions.explain: amount <= 0 catches both zero and negative amounts. Zero is the input people forget; a negative transfer would silently reverse the direction of the money.
questions.expected: Refused: the amount must be more than 0

questions.q: This program finds the problem but moves the money anyway. Change it so the money only moves when problem is "none". It must print A: 5000 B: 1000.
questions.explain: A check is useless if the next piece ignores it. Wrapping the move in if (problem === "none") is the join between the two pieces: exactly the kind of place where real bugs hide.

questions.q: Withdrawals and transfers should follow the same rule: a member may use their whole balance. The transfer copy of the rule is wrong. Fix it so the program prints Withdrawal: allowed and then Transfer: allowed.
questions.explain: Both copies must use <=. Better still, once you know functions, the rule would live in one shared piece so the two can never drift apart again.

questions.q: Build the fee piece: ₦10 for amounts up to ₦5,000, ₦25 up to ₦50,000, and ₦50 above that. For the amount given, it must print Fee: ₦25.
questions.explain: Check the smallest band first. ₦20,000 is not up to ₦5,000, but it is up to ₦50,000, so the fee is ₦25. Test the piece at 5,000, 5,001, 50,000 and 50,001 too.

questions.q: A member may send at most ₦100,000 per day in total. Write the check so that, with the inputs given, the program prints over the daily limit. When the total is ₦100,000 or less it should print allowed.
questions.explain: The piece needs only two numbers. ₦70,000 + ₦35,000 is ₦105,000, more than the limit. "At most ₦100,000" means exactly ₦100,000 is still allowed, so the condition uses >.

questions.q: The same request, TX-9, arrives twice, and the money moves twice. Remember the last reference and skip a request whose reference was already done. It must print Sent. Balance: 35000 and then Already done: TX-9.
questions.explain: This is the leaf the first transfer tree forgot. Real systems store every reference they have processed, not just the last one, but the idea is the same: the same request must not move money twice.

questions.q: Tunde tries to send more than Ada has from Ada's account. The checks are in the wrong order, so the message tells him Ada's balance is too low. Reorder them so it prints Refused: you do not own this account.
questions.explain: Only the first failing check is reported. Checking ownership first means a stranger learns nothing about someone else's account. The order of the leaves is part of the design.
questions.expected: Refused: you do not own this account
